Markup vs Margin for Contractors: How to Price Without Losing Money

Published 19 November 2026

Markup is your profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is your profit as a percentage of the selling price. On an item that costs you RM100, a 30% markup gives a selling price of RM130, but your margin is only 23.1%. To earn a true 30% margin you’d need to sell at RM142.86. Mixing the two up is one of the quietest ways contractors underquote. Below are the formulas, two conversion tables and worked examples.

The formulas

Formula
Selling price with a markup cost × (1 + markup)
Selling price for a target margin cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Markup → margin markup ÷ (1 + markup)
Margin → markup margin ÷ (1 − margin)
Margin on a line (selling price − cost) ÷ selling price

Markup to margin

Markup on cost Selling price on RM100 cost Margin
10% RM110.00 9.1%
15% RM115.00 13.0%
20% RM120.00 16.7%
25% RM125.00 20.0%
30% RM130.00 23.1%
40% RM140.00 28.6%
50% RM150.00 33.3%
100% RM200.00 50.0%

Margin to markup

Target margin Selling price on RM100 cost Markup needed
10% RM111.11 11.1%
15% RM117.65 17.6%
20% RM125.00 25.0%
25% RM133.33 33.3%
30% RM142.86 42.9%
35% RM153.85 53.8%
40% RM166.67 66.7%

Why it matters on a real job

Say a renovation costs you RM50,000 in materials, labour and subcontractors, and you want a 30% margin to cover overheads and profit:

Pricing Selling price Profit Actual margin
30% markup (cost × 1.30) RM65,000 RM15,000 23.1%
30% margin (cost ÷ 0.70) RM71,428.57 RM21,428.57 30.0%

The gap is RM6,428.57 on a single job. If your overheads (rent, vehicles, staff, insurance) take 15% of sales, the 30% markup leaves about 8% profit, while the true 30% margin leaves about 15%.

Margin by line, not just in total

A quotation’s overall margin can look healthy while individual lines lose money. Common culprits:

  • Carpentry priced from an old supplier rate after board prices went up.
  • Subcontracted trades (plumbing, aircon, glass) passed through with little or no markup.
  • Small “lot” items like protection, disposal and cleaning, priced from memory.
  • Discounts given on the total, which come straight out of margin.

Checking cost and selling price on every line before you send catches these. On an item that costs RM100 and sells for RM142.86 (a 30% margin), a RM10 discount cuts the margin to about 25%.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Saying “30%” without saying which. Decide whether your target is markup or margin, and write it down for your team.
  • Adding markup to a discounted total. Work out the discount’s effect on margin before agreeing to it.
  • Forgetting overheads. Margin has to pay for rent, vehicles, admin time and defects, not just profit.
  • Not updating costs. A rate that made 30% last year may make 20% today.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between markup and margin?
Markup is your profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is your profit as a percentage of the selling price. On an item that costs RM100 and sells for RM130, the markup is 30% but the margin is only 23.1%.
How do I convert markup to margin?
Margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). For example, a 30% markup gives 0.30 ÷ 1.30 = 23.1% margin. To go the other way, markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin).
How do I price for a 30% margin?
Divide your cost by (1 − 0.30), which is 0.70. An item that costs RM100 must sell for RM142.86 to earn a 30% margin. Multiplying the cost by 1.30 only gives a 23.1% margin.
Should a contractor use markup or margin?
Either works, as long as you use one consistently and know which one you mean. Many contractors price with markup because it's quick, but set targets and check jobs using margin, because overheads and profit are paid out of the selling price.
